signals_systems.question: What is the difference between a continuous-time and a discrete-time signal, and name two properties of a sinusoid.
signals_systems.reference_answer: Continuous-time signals are defined for every instant on the real line; discrete-time signals are defined only at sampling instants nT. A sinusoid is characterised by amplitude, frequency, and phase.
rubric_points: Two of amplitude, frequency, phase (1 pt)
Clear wording, not only labels (1 pt)

sampling_theorem.question: State the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem and explain what aliasing is.
sampling_theorem.reference_answer: To reconstruct a bandlimited signal, sample at more than twice the highest frequency (Nyquist rate). Aliasing is high-frequency content folding into lower frequencies when this rate is violated.
rubric_points: Aliasing as frequency fold-over / misidentification (1 pt)

fourier_series.question: What does a Fourier series represent, and for what class of signals is it typically used?
fourier_series.reference_answer: A Fourier series decomposes a periodic signal into a sum of sinusoids (or complex exponentials) at harmonic frequencies. It applies to periodic signals that meet Dirichlet conditions.

fourier_transform.question: How does the Fourier transform relate the time and frequency domains?
fourier_transform.reference_answer: The Fourier transform represents a (generally aperiodic) time signal as a continuum of frequency components. Magnitude shows which frequencies are present; phase encodes alignment. Inverse transform recovers the time signal.

dft_fft.question: What is the DFT, and why is the FFT used in practice?
dft_fft.reference_answer: The DFT is the discrete, finite-length version of the Fourier transform on N samples. Direct DFT is O(N^2); the FFT computes the same result in O(N log N), making real-time spectral analysis practical.
rubric_points: DFT as discrete frequency samples of a finite sequence (1 pt)
FFT is a fast algorithm for the DFT (1 pt)

filtering_basics.question: What does a low-pass filter do, and what is a cutoff frequency?
filtering_basics.reference_answer: A low-pass filter attenuates frequencies above a cutoff and passes those below. Cutoff is typically the frequency where gain drops by 3 dB. High-pass and band-pass are defined analogously.
rubric_points: Passes low / attenuates high (or equivalent for another type if clearly stated) (1 pt)
Names another filter type or order/roll-off (1 pt)

convolution.question: What does convolution of a signal with a filter impulse response represent?
convolution.reference_answer: Discrete convolution y[n] = x[n]*h[n] is the output of a linear time-invariant system with impulse response h. For FIR filters, output samples are weighted sums of current and past inputs.

windowing.question: What is spectral leakage, and why do we apply a window before an FFT?
windowing.reference_answer: Finite-length truncation is like multiplying by a rectangle, whose spectrum smears energy into neighbouring bins (leakage). Tapered windows (Hann, Hamming, Blackman) reduce side lobes at the cost of wider main lobes.
rubric_points: Names a window or trade-off (1 pt)

stft_spectrogram.question: Why use an STFT or spectrogram instead of a single FFT for a speech or music signal?
stft_spectrogram.reference_answer: A single FFT assumes stationarity over the whole record. Non-stationary signals change over time; the STFT computes FFTs on successive windowed frames so a spectrogram can show how frequency content evolves.
rubric_points: Trade-off time vs frequency resolution (optional but credit if present) or example (1 pt)

noise_snr.question: What is SNR, and name one practical way to improve it.
noise_snr.reference_answer: Signal-to-noise ratio is the ratio of signal power to noise power, often in decibels. Averaging repeated measurements, band-limiting with a filter, or shielding/grounding can raise SNR.
rubric_points: Signal power relative to noise (1 pt)
Averaging, filtering, or another valid method (1 pt)
